title: trivialbaselines: zero-image null models for slice-labelled medical imaging benchmarks

creators.name: Raut, Aditya
creators.affiliation: Neuqua Valley High School, Naperville, Illinois

description:
A benchmark auditor that reads no pixels. Given only a label table — subject identifier, slice index, label, and split — it reports how much of a published performance number is reachable without any image data: from where a slice sits in its stack, from acquisition or release metadata, from volume size, or from prevalence alone.

Each baseline is reported at both slice and patient level with subject-clustered bootstrap intervals, and is calibrated against its own permutation null rather than against an assumed 0.5 — a metadata baseline fitted out-of-fold on a subject-level label sits systematically below 0.5, so judging against 0.5 would manufacture spurious below-chance findings.

Requires numpy and pandas only. No images, no GPU, and no data-use agreement covering pixel data, which is what makes third-party auditing of benchmarks one does not hold possible at all.

Worked result. On the published label file and patient-disjoint split of a 2024 prostate diffusion MRI classification study, the positional baseline reaches 0.851 (95% CI 0.816–0.887) slice-level AUROC against a reported 0.809–0.861, and falls to 0.424 (0.298–0.547) at the patient level. Roughly 98% of the published margin over chance requires no pixels.

Prior art, stated plainly. The construction is not novel and this package does not claim it. A position-only baseline was publicly disclosed in a 2020 Kaggle notebook (“Baseline with no image”, RSNA-STR Pulmonary Embolism Detection), and a location-only baseline appears in DeepLesion's own defining paper (Yan et al., CVPR 2018). Metadata-driven performance was demonstrated by Badgeley et al. (npj Digital Medicine, 2019). What is contributed here is a reusable implementation with confidence intervals, the slice-versus-patient contrast, and permutation calibration.

Verification. The self-test includes a benchmark the baselines must fail to detect — a genuinely image-driven label — alongside ones they must detect, so a tool that always fires cannot pass.
